# Take Gifts From the Richest Pile.

@example 100 drops to 10, then 30 to 5, then 10 to 3, leaving 5 + 5 + 3 + 2.
[30,5,100,2]
3
=> 15

@example The first round turns the 2 into 1. From then on every pile holds 1, and a pile of 1 never shrinks, so the last five rounds change nothing.
[1,2,1]
6
=> 3

@example The only pile is chosen twice: 81 becomes 9, then 3.
[81]
2
=> 3

# The smallest input.
[1]
1
=> 1

# The largest pile: floor(sqrt(10^9)) = 31622.
[1000000000]
1
=> 31622

# 31622^2 = 999950884 and one less, where a single-precision square root
# rounds the wrong way.
[999950884]
1
=> 31622

[999950883]
1
=> 31621

# 31621^2 - 1 = 999887640.
[999887640]
1
=> 31620

# The total (5 * 10^9 + 31622) needs more than 32 bits.
[1000000000,1000000000,1000000000,1000000000,1000000000,1000000000]
1
=> 5000031622

# The same pile stays the largest for three rounds:
# 10^9 -> 31622 -> 177 -> 13.
[1000000000,2]
3
=> 15

# The largest pile must be found again each round: after 100 drops to 10,
# 10 is still larger than 8, so it drops to 3.
[8,100]
2
=> 11

# Ties: two of the three 16s drop to 4.
[16,16,16]
2
=> 24

# More rounds than are useful: everything ends at 1.
[4,9,1]
10
=> 3

# The most rounds on one huge pile.
[1000000000]
1000
=> 1

# Random small cases from gen.c (lc check --regen makes them).
@gen 1 small
[14,38261,11916303]
7
=> 13

@gen 2 small
[9,5,19,839324398,521463258]
6
=> 58

@gen 3 small
[7,4,31822,583160443,5,4532]
11
=> 19

@gen 4 small
[31521,903926342]
8
=> 4

@gen 5 small
[95643,362217024,3532,595379912]
2
=> 142607

@gen 6 small
[322214082,69775528,2,371063168]
10
=> 25
